strengths: Systematic and rigorous survey methodology following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, including a comprehensive PRISMA flow diagram, search string sensitivity analysis, and quantified inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha).

A well-structured and conceptually clear multidimensional taxonomy that effectively disentangles attribution paradigms (parametric vs. non-parametric), citation characteristics (modality, granularity level, style, visibility, frequency), and generation tasks.

Comprehensive and insightful synthesis of the evaluation ecosystem, categorizing 300 metrics across seven dimensions and six calculation methods, successfully highlighting the acute fragmentation and reuse bottleneck (e.g., only two frameworks reused across the surveyed corpus).
Actionable and practically useful evaluation guidelines (Table 1 and Table 9) that explicitly map out when and why specific metrics should be used based on task formulation and evidence availability.
Remarkably detailed appendices providing an exhaustive annotated matrix of all 134 surveyed papers (Table 7), metric comparisons, and summaries of benchmarks, frameworks, and datasets.
weaknesses: The survey is purely descriptive and meta-analytic; it does not include empirical experiments or meta-evaluations benchmarking existing metrics or frameworks on a shared testbed.

While the title and motivation prominently feature 'Quotation' alongside 'Attribution' and 'Citation', quotation receives noticeably less structural depth throughout the taxonomy and analysis, primarily being relegated to a minor citation style and specific prompting/training tricks.

The literature cut-off date (February 2025) means rapidly emerging developments regarding long-form reasoning models (e.g., test-time compute, native search/grounding tokens in reasoning-oriented LLMs) are only briefly touched upon.

strengths: Methodological rigor and transparency: The survey adheres strictly to the PRISMA protocol for systematic mapping studies, clearly documenting search strings, inclusion/exclusion criteria, screening procedures, inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha across all taxonomy dimensions), and a sensitivity analysis.

Comprehensive and cohesive taxonomy: The paper successfully synthesizes a fragmented literature landscape into an intuitive facetted classification covering attribution paradigms (parametric vs. non-parametric variants), citation characteristics (modality, granularity, style, visibility, frequency), tasks, and LLM integration mechanisms.

Thorough and actionable evaluation taxonomy: Systematically categorizes 300 metrics across seven evaluation dimensions and six evaluation methods, accompanied by concrete guidelines (Table 1) and a comparative analysis of trade-offs and failure modes for core metrics (Table 9).

Extensive bibliographic and resource mapping: The appendix provides exhaustive annotations of all 134 reviewed papers, alongside comprehensive mappings of reused frameworks, benchmarks, and datasets, serving as an outstanding reference repository for the NLP community.
weaknesses: The primary keyword query ('large language model'/'llm' AND 'citation'/'attribution'/'quote') relies heavily on explicit terminology. While the sensitivity analysis indicates strong recall, some earlier or adjacent work framed purely around 'grounded generation', 'source verification', or 'fact-checking' without these explicit keywords might have been bypassed.

Because of page constraints and the broad scope of mapping 134 papers and 300 metrics, the technical and algorithmic details of specific modeling techniques (e.g., exact loss formulations or decoding-time constraints) are discussed at a high level rather than through deep mechanistic comparisons.

strengths: Highly systematic and methodologically rigorous literature review following the PRISMA 2020 protocol, including transparent search queries, database coverage, a sensitivity analysis, and reported inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha) for both screening and taxonomy labeling.
Provides a clear and well-structured taxonomy that consolidates fragmented terminology across attribution, citation, and quotation in evidence-based LLM generation.

Comprehensive analysis of evaluation practices, categorizing 300 metrics across 7 evaluation dimensions and 6 methods, supplemented by actionable guidelines (Table 1) and a detailed limitations/applicability matrix for core metrics (Table 9).
Extensive and high-utility appendix providing full annotations for all 134 surveyed papers across taxonomy dimensions, as well as systematic breakdowns of frameworks, benchmarks, and datasets.
weaknesses: As a systematic survey paper, the work does not introduce novel empirical models or run new benchmark experiments, relying purely on meta-synthesis of existing literature.

The boundary between certain non-parametric categories (e.g., 'in-context' attribution versus 'post-retrieval' attribution) can occasionally blur in practical systems where retrieved documents are simply prepended to the context window.

With the literature search conducted in February 2025, recent developments around native chain-of-thought reasoning models (e.g., specialized reasoning LLMs performing dynamic tool use and search grounding) are only sparsely touched upon.

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: The paper consolidates a rapidly growing and fragmented research field (evidence-based text generation, attribution, citation, and quotation), where over 86% of the surveyed works were published after 2023.

Systematic and rigorous mapping methodology: The literature search follows established systematic mapping guidelines (Petersen et al., 2008) across nine major databases, applying clear inclusion/exclusion criteria and multi-annotator screening.

Comprehensive and coherent taxonomy: The paper provides a clear framework categorizing attribution approaches (refining parametric vs. non-parametric with in-generation and in-context classes), LLM integration techniques, citation characteristics (granularity, modality, style, frequency, visibility), and tasks.

In-depth analysis of evaluation practices: The survey systematically classifies 300 evaluation metrics across seven dimensions and six computation methods, pinpointing the acute lack of standardized benchmark reuse in the literature.
Clarity and presentation: The manuscript is well structured, easy to read, and supported by informative figures and summary tables (e.g., Figures 4 and 7; Tables 3, 5, and 6).
weaknesses: Potential recall limitations in the search string: Requiring ('large language model' OR 'llm') AND ('citation' OR 'attribution' OR 'quote') strictly in the title and abstract may omit closely related work on verifiability, provenance, faithful RAG, or grounded dialog that uses alternative phrasing (e.g., 'source grounding', 'faithfulness verification', 'evidence tracing').

Primarily descriptive mapping rather than deep technical meta-analysis: The paper functions mainly as a bibliometric and taxonomic mapping study; it offers limited quantitative comparison of empirical performance, trade-offs, computational overhead, or failure cases among representative methods on standard benchmarks.

Limited depth on practical system bottlenecks: The discussion could more thoroughly analyze practical engineering challenges, such as inference latency introduced by in-generation retrieval, context compression constraints, and vulnerabilities to citation hallucination or adversarial evidence manipulation.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated topic: As large language models are increasingly deployed in knowledge-intensive domains, ensuring output traceability and verifiability via attribution, citation, and quotation is a critical area of NLP research.

Methodological rigor in literature collection: The paper follows formal systematic mapping guidelines (Petersen et al., 2008), querying nine major computer science and NLP databases with clearly articulated inclusion and screening criteria.

Clear and comprehensive taxonomy: The survey introduces a structured taxonomy spanning attribution paradigms (expanding prior parametric/non-parametric distinctions to include in-generation and in-context approaches), LLM integration modes, citation characteristics (granularity, styles, visibility), and downstream tasks.

Extensive cataloging of evaluation practices: The systematization of 300 evaluation metrics across seven dimensions and six calculation methods, alongside an audit of 17 frameworks and 11 benchmarks, effectively highlights the fragmentation and lack of standardization currently facing the community.
weaknesses: Search string constraints and potential literature omission: The search string `("large language model" OR "llm") AND ("citation" OR "attribution" OR "quote")` matched strictly on title and abstract. This runs the risk of omitting closely related and influential work on grounded generation, source grounding, provenance, and factual verification that might frame their contributions around terms like 'grounding', 'provenance', or 'evidence alignment' rather than explicit citation/attribution keywords.

Predominantly descriptive synthesis rather than critical technical comparison: A substantial portion of the paper is dedicated to reporting distributional statistics (e.g., percentages of studies using zero-shot prompting vs. fine-tuning, paragraph-level vs. document-level citations) rather than deeply comparing technical mechanisms, trade-offs, failure modes, or synthesizing empirical findings across different model families and architectures.

Brevity of future outlook and open challenges: The discussion in Section 7 touches on three challenges (parametric attribution, evaluation standardization, explainable citations) in less than one page, leaving out several pressing practical and theoretical problems such as real-time latency/cost trade-offs in iterative in-generation retrieval, robustness under conflicting or noisy sources, and copyright/intellectual property considerations surrounding direct quotations.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated survey addressing the fragmentation in terminology, methodology, and evaluation across evidence-based and attributed text generation with LLMs.
Rigorous and transparent methodology based on established systematic mapping guidelines (Petersen et al., 2008), surveying 134 papers, 300 metrics, 17 frameworks, and 231 datasets.

Comprehensive and clear taxonomy covering attribution mechanisms (parametric vs. non-parametric), LLM integration strategies, granular citation characteristics (modality, level, style, visibility, frequency), and generation tasks.

In-depth systematization of evaluation practices (Section 6 and Figure 7), successfully mapping metrics across seven evaluation dimensions and six evaluation methods, exposing the lack of benchmark reusability in current literature.
Commitment to open science by providing the full annotated literature dataset in a public repository.
weaknesses: The literature search query ('large language model' OR 'llm') matched only against title and abstract appears overly restrictive, missing foundational papers in attributed generation that do not use these exact terms (e.g., WebGPT by Nakano et al., 2021).

The survey focuses heavily on bibliometric mapping and classification statistics (counts and percentages) at the expense of deeper algorithmic and technical analysis of the underlying mechanisms (e.g., loss functions, decoding constraints, or attention intervention).

Lack of empirical synthesis or cross-paper comparison regarding the actual performance, latency trade-offs, and failure modes (such as hallucinated citations, broken links, or attribution misplacement) across the categorized approaches.
Several figures (notably Figure 4 and Figure 7) suffer from very small text and high visual density, compromising readability in standard print/screen layout.
